title: Individual productivity triples, company delivery only goes from 20 days to 17
dek: AI armed everyone, but the organization didn't get faster — because the weakest plank in the barrel isn't a person, it's a process. The real dividing line is whether you can rework processes and the organization, not whether you hand out tokens to employees.
why: A frontline CEO talks concretely about building his own CEO AI, canceling weekly meetings, and using token consumption to identify elite performers — the mechanisms and numbers are specific, and the decision-hub section in the back half is the most valuable.
who: CEOs, CTOs and HR leads at companies pushing AI adoption, especially managers trying to figure out why individual productivity went up but the organization didn't get faster.
skip: The first 4 minutes of education-scenario setup can be fast-forwarded; go straight to the barrel's weakest-plank case at 16:07.

points.h: Individual productivity triples, delivery only gets three days faster
points.body: NetEase ran the numbers last year: a software requirement, from the product manager receiving it and producing design mockups to the feature going live, averaged 20 working days. After AI coding crossed the inflection point, many engineers doubled or even tripled-to-quintupled their individual efficiency, some tenfold. But for features of the same scope, the whole process only shrank from 20 days to 17. The reason is that a team completing a complex task is like a barrel: of 20 planks, 10 are engineers, 3 are product, 3 are testing. The engineer and product manager planks shoot up fast, but some planks aren't people at all — they're processes, and they didn't improve at all. So AI adoption has to clear three hurdles: cognition, landing on individual short-range tasks, and reworking processes and the organization — the third is the hardest.

points.h: Cancel the weekly meeting: AI syncs information, humans only solve problems
points.body: Ruan Liang asked friends who run companies whether they still hold weekly meetings; 99% said yes. Weekly meetings usually serve three purposes: sync information, spot problems and opportunities, and make decisions. It used to be 2.5 hours a week, but the time spent on that meeting could be ten times 2.5 hours — every department prepares materials layer by layer, and the information sync itself wasn't done well, because nobody listens attentively the whole time and may miss the one sentence relevant to them. After the reform: the general manager and management agree on what information is needed, everyone fills in a template and stores it in the knowledge base, and AI scans and integrates it into a focused, interactive HTML report that people can leave comments and follow-up questions on; an AI agent produces a list of problems and opportunities in advance, and human brains confirm and supplement; solving problems and making decisions move to dedicated meetings.

points.h: SaaS isn't dead, but ordinary SaaS will die
points.body: Ruan Liang doesn't think SaaS is dead: SaaS is essentially Service, and Service always exists, it just changes form — AI as a Service and Agent as a Service are themselves software. But ordinary SaaS may really die, while genuinely good SaaS that has already entered a company's critical processes will only get better, because it becomes internal infrastructure. In the past, humans used software, limited by time and energy; in the future, large numbers of agents will call databases, APIs, security APIs, review APIs, HR APIs, CRM APIs — call volumes far exceeding the number and actions of humans, growing enormously, and the more it's called the more entrenched it becomes. The premise is that the Service itself is critical enough inside the company.

points.h: Distill top salespeople into skills and distribute them to everyone
points.body: Bosses have two headaches: the sales team has only one or two strong performers and the rest are mediocre; or a salesperson is so strong that if they leave, what then. There used to be no way, but now you can distill or extract a good salesperson's moves, scripts and behaviors into skills. Two uses: distribute them to other salespeople to use directly; and have AI turn elite salespeople into teachers who train ordinary salespeople. What training should distill isn't the salesperson, it's the customer — take the customer interaction data a salesperson has touched, like calls, WeChat, emails, and have AI simulate various customers to train salespeople. Online sales is purely digital and on record; for offline sales, recommend or even require a recording card — after a visit, while memory is fresh, record two or three minutes of voice notes, because salespeople dislike CRM (they think CRM is for managing them) but don't mind a recording card, since it's also useful for their own customer review.

points.h: Fewer middle managers, strong individuals return to the front line with agent legions
points.body: Ruan Liang judges that middle managers will become fewer and fewer, but not necessarily because they're eliminated — rather, they go to the front line, and the front line can also lead a bunch of agents. Middle managers performing management duties will become fewer and fewer, while elite people with powerful skills will become more and more. He gives the example of an engineering team: previously, socialized division of labor split software development ever finer — frontend, backend, algorithm, test engineers; in the last half year it has clearly reverted to full-stack, everyone becoming full-end engineers. In the future the organization will look more and more like a distributed-peak structure, with countless strong engineers, one mother peak commanding some engineers, and countless agents fighting a battle. He imagines a future interview negotiation scene: the candidate says I'm not one person, I bring an AI team, a summary of all my past experience and skills, and the premium the company has to pay might be some kind of OPC.

points.h: AI value formula: quality times time saved
points.body: Ruan Liang gives a formula referencing a paper: AI's value = the quality of AI completing the task (as a ratio of human quality) × time saved × the company's economic value per unit time. For example, a human makes a cup of coffee at eight out of ten, AI also makes it at eight out of ten, so the quality coefficient is 1; a human takes 20 minutes, AI takes only 10 seconds, saving 14 minutes 50 seconds; multiply by the company's economic value per unit time and you can calculate ROI. Prioritize four kinds of tasks for AI: ones that take time, are high-frequency, are unavoidable, and produce roughly the same result regardless of who does them. Once calculated, you can immediately decide whether to use AI. He also suggests first using the most expensive AI (Cloud, GPT) to prove the thing can be done, solidify the process, then switch to cheaper ones — if the most expensive can do it, within two months the cheap ones can too.

points.h: Token consumption leads by a landslide, output also leads by a landslide
points.body: NetEase started a points system in 2024, trying to quantify engineers' work tasks into points with work value. By the AI era they found a type of person whose token consumption is astonishing, and whose work output and work value are also astonishing, forming a statistical pattern: people whose token consumption leads by a landslide are most likely building systems for themselves, saving their own work time and increasing thinking time, so their work quality and work results also lead by a landslide. Many bosses worry about waste from AI abuse; Ruan Liang's hot take is that truly excellent or elite people don't waste — the company has audits but doesn't tell colleagues, and through statistics they found elite colleagues don't waste. He also says small companies more easily embrace AI thoroughly, because there are fewer organizational relationships, the boss uses it first, the hierarchy is shallow, and the chain is short.

points.h: The core of a decision hub is decision history, not the model
points.body: Building an AI decision hub essentially requires a high-quality knowledge base, and what really matters is the historical decision processes and decision bases. This year NetEase preserved decisions that happened historically, brought them into the knowledge base, combined the two types of knowledge to train an agent or skill, then fed the original several hundred cases back in for the agent to judge, achieving accuracy above 90%. Ruan Liang also mentions that Bridgewater gave researchers and analysts an agent it built itself, precipitating decision processes and decision history into a decision knowledge base; what Bridgewater did better was making the agent a learnable, evolvable part — after a person adjusts it, the confirmed adjustment action enters the next round of reinforcement, keeping pace with the times, equivalent to human-machine collaborative self-evolution.
